title: Judges 1:1–8
context: After Joshua’s death, the children of Israel ask the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites. The LORD answers that Judah shall go up, for he has delivered the land into Judah’s hand. Judah invites Simeon to fight in his lot and promises to do the same in Simeon’s. The LORD delivers the Canaanites and the Perizzites; they strike ten thousand men in Bezek, seize Adoni-Bezek, and cut off his thumbs and his big toes. He himself says that God has done to him as he had done to seventy kings. They bring him to Jerusalem, where he dies. Judah then fights against Jerusalem, takes it, strikes it with the edge of the sword, and sets the city on fire. Both traditions read the unit as a beginning under God’s word: Israel inquires, and the early victories are credited to the LORD’s delivery. How this taking of Jerusalem in verse 8 relates to the Jebusites still living there in verse 21 is a long-noticed tension; readers have offered several explanations, and none should be treated as a settled consensus. The inquiry, the LORD’s answer, and the LORD’s delivery are shared ground.

verses.text: After the death of Joshua, the children of Israel asked of the LORD, saying, “Who should go up for us first against the Canaanites, to fight against them?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The book opens “After the death of Joshua,” and the children of Israel ask the LORD, “Who should go up for us first against the Canaanites, to fight against them?” They do not simply rush the next campaign; they inquire.

Arminian readers hear a genuine asking. The people must wait for the LORD’s answer and then actually go up under it; the question is a real act of dependence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise stress that the first move after Joshua’s death is a question put to the LORD. The conquest is not restarted by Israel’s own plan; they seek his direction for who should go first.

Both traditions take the verse as inquiry rather than presumption, shared ground at the book’s opening.

verses.text: The LORD said, “Judah shall go up. Behold, I have delivered the land into his hand.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD said, “Judah shall go up. Behold, I have delivered the land into his hand.” Judah’s advance is commanded, and the land is spoken of as already delivered.

Arminian readers hear a clear word that Judah must now obey. The gift is God’s, and the tribe is really called to go up and take what he has delivered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the perfect grant: “I have delivered the land into his hand.” Judah goes up because God has already given; the command rests on that delivery.

Both traditions read the answer as God’s own appointment of Judah and as his gift of the land, not as a merely human choice of a lead tribe.

verses.text: Judah said to Simeon his brother, “Come up with me into my lot, that we may fight against the Canaanites; and I likewise will go with you into your lot.” So Simeon went with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah said to Simeon his brother, “Come up with me into my lot, that we may fight against the Canaanites; and I likewise will go with you into your lot.” So Simeon went with him.

Arminian readers hear a real partnership under the word of verse 2. Judah does not go alone; the brothers bind themselves to help one another in the portions already allotted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the invitation as cooperation within the lots God has assigned, not as a substitute for the LORD’s delivery already spoken.

Both traditions take the verse as brotherly help in the allotted inheritance, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: Judah went up, and the LORD delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand. They struck ten thousand men in Bezek.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah went up, “and the LORD delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand.” They struck ten thousand men in Bezek.

Arminian readers hear obedience meeting God’s help. Judah actually goes up, and the victory is credited to the LORD’s delivery, not to Judah’s numbers alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same clause: it is the LORD who delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand. The ten thousand fall under that gift.

Both traditions take the success at Bezek as the LORD’s doing. The site’s exact location is discussed; the verse itself names the place and the deliverer, and that is enough here.

verses.text: They found Adoni-Bezek in Bezek, and they fought against him. They struck the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
verses.arminianNotes:
They found Adoni-Bezek in Bezek, fought against him, and struck the Canaanites and the Perizzites. The campaign of verse 4 now closes on the city’s lord.

Arminian readers hear a concrete pursuit of the fight God had delivered into their hand. The named opponent is found and engaged; the battle is not left as a vague report.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the finding and the fighting as the outworking of the LORD’s delivery already stated. Adoni-Bezek is met in his own place and struck down with his people.

Both traditions read the verse as the particular victory that verse 6 will complete, on shared ground.

verses.text: But Adoni-Bezek fled. They pursued him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.
verses.arminianNotes:
Adoni-Bezek fled. They pursued him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his big toes. The mutilation is a humiliating disablement of a warrior.

Arminian readers do not hurry past the harshness of the act. The text reports what Israel did; verse 7 will give the king’s own reading of it, and the narrator does not pause here to praise or to blame the method.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise let the report stand. Pursuit, capture, and this particular cruelty prepare for Adoni-Bezek’s confession in the next verse, rather than for a separate debate between the two traditions.

Both take the verse as narrative fact, the prelude to his words about God’s recompense.

verses.text: Adoni-Bezek said, “Seventy kings, having their thumbs and their big toes cut off, scavenged under my table. As I have done, so God has done to me.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
verses.arminianNotes:
Adoni-Bezek said, “Seventy kings, having their thumbs and their big toes cut off, scavenged under my table. As I have done, so God has done to me.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.

Arminian readers hear even this Canaanite lord acknowledging a just return. He names God as the one who has done to him what he had done to others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same confession: “As I have done, so God has done to me.” The recompense is referred to God, not merely to Judah’s revenge, and he is then brought to Jerusalem, where he dies.

Both traditions take his words as a recognition of measure for measure under God, shared ground in a grim scene.

verses.text: The children of Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire. The verse reports a real taking and burning.

Arminian readers hear a decisive strike, and they also hold it beside verse 21, where Jebusites still inhabit Jerusalem. How a city taken and burned here is later held by Jebusites is an old question, not a point on which the two traditions divide.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the taking and the fire as the text states them, without forcing one explanation of the later notice in verse 21. Suggested readings include a temporary capture, a success that was not a lasting occupation, or different parts or stages of the city; none of these is a demonstrated consensus.

Both traditions refuse to flatten either verse, and they treat the tension as an interpretive issue, not as an Arminian–Reformed contrast.
